pages.title: GPT-6.1 Sol vs GPT-6 Astra: API Prices & Evaluation | KeyoAPI
pages.metaDescription: Compare GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Astra on KeyoAPI: input/output token prices, a worked request budget, model IDs and an API evaluation checklist.
pages.lead: Choosing between GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Astra starts with the price of a successful task. Both are listed on KeyoAPI with the same OpenAI-compatible chat endpoint; Sol costs one fifth as much per token in the default billing group. Compare answer quality and retries on your own workload before choosing a default.

sections.heading: GPT 6.1 Sol pricing vs GPT 6 Astra
paragraphs: The rates below were checked against KeyoAPI's public pricing catalog on 2026-10-13. They are KeyoAPI sell rates for the default group, not a statement of OpenAI's official list prices. Other billing groups can apply a multiplier. Cached input, extra modalities and different billing modes require their own rate check.
paragraphsAfter: For 1,000 requests with that same token mix, the planning total is $7.354 for Sol or $36.770 for Astra before retries and additional charges. Cost = input tokens / 1,000,000 × input rate + output tokens / 1,000,000 × output rate. These figures use more precision than the rounded model-guide labels.

sections.heading: When does the higher Astra rate pay off?
paragraphs: Start a Sol evaluation with the tasks you actually ship: product Q&A, structured extraction, code edits or document summaries. Keep the prompts and required outputs fixed. Test Astra on the same cases and measure whether it resolves failures that Sol leaves unfinished. A model name or higher rate alone does not establish a quality advantage.

Score correctness, schema validity, completed tasks, latency and total billed tokens including retries. A fivefold unit-price difference means Astra needs a measurable benefit in your workload to justify routing every request to it. A practical alternative is a Sol default with Astra reserved for cases rejected by your validators; verify that the second attempt improves the result rather than repeating the first failure.

sections.heading: Use the exact API model IDs
paragraphs: Use gpt-6.1-sol for GPT 6.1 Sol (sometimes written GPT Sol 6.1), and gpt-6-astra for Astra. Keep the same endpoint, API key and messages when you compare them. Do not substitute a search phrase such as gpt-sol-6.1 for the catalog ID. Tool calling, context limits and optional parameters should be checked for the specific route before integration.
sections.code:
curl https://www.keyoapi.xyz/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEYO_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model":"gpt-6.1-sol","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Summarize this project brief in three actionable steps: ship a search feature, evaluate relevance, and report costs."}],"max_tokens":400}'

faqs.q: Is GPT-6.1 Sol five times cheaper than GPT-6 Astra?
faqs.a: In the checked default-group token rates, yes: both input and output cost one fifth as much. Total task cost can differ because the models may produce different output lengths or require different retry counts.

faqs.q: Which model is better for coding?
faqs.a: The catalog prices do not answer that. Compare accepted patches, passing tests, completion rate and cost per accepted result on the same repository tasks. Use those results to choose your routing policy.

faqs.q: Where can I verify the current GPT 6.1 Sol price?
faqs.a: See /model/gpt-6.1-sol for the model guide and /pricing for the live catalog. The broader rate table is on /openai-api-pricing.

pages.lead: Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5 are two distinct Claude-class catalog IDs on KeyoAPI. The default-group rate for Fable is about 4.17 times the Opus rate. Use the cost table to budget an evaluation, then compare completed work instead of assuming the more expensive option is better for every task.

sections.heading: Opus 5.5 vs Fable 5.1 API pricing
paragraphs: Checked against KeyoAPI's public catalog on 2026-10-13. These are KeyoAPI sell rates for the default billing group, not Anthropic official list prices. The examples cover ordinary input and output tokens; they exclude cached-token differences, extra modalities, billing-group multipliers and retries.
paragraphsAfter: For 1,000 requests at that mix, plan $35.294 for Opus or $147.060 for Fable before retries and additional charges. A long agent session may send its growing conversation repeatedly, so estimate the tokens across every turn rather than only the final answer.

sections.heading: Choose a model for coding and agent tasks
paragraphs: Build an evaluation set with your actual acceptance rules: a patch must pass the project tests, a research answer must cite the supplied sources, and a plan must respect its constraints. Give both models the same instructions, context, execution budget and available tools. Record successful tasks, human corrections and the bill for the entire session.

Consider Opus as a lower-cost candidate in this pair and Fable as an option to test on difficult failures. That is a cost-based experiment, not a benchmark claim. Fable is economical only when its measured improvement in accepted results or avoided retries compensates for the higher unit rate. Keep a task and token budget so either model stops after repeated failures.

faqs.q: Does Fable 5.1 cost more than Opus 5.5?
faqs.a: At the checked default-group rates, Fable input and output tokens each cost about 4.17 times as much. Use actual session usage to calculate your task cost.

faqs.q: Are these official Anthropic model names and prices?

pages.title: AI Agent API: Build Bounded Workflows with One Key | KeyoAPI
pages.h1: Build an AI agent with the KeyoAPI chat API
pages.metaDescription: Build an AI agent using KeyoAPI's chat API: separate planning from execution, validate tool actions, set turn budgets and compare model costs per completed task.
pages.lead: An AI agent combines model requests with application code that tracks state, runs tools and checks results. KeyoAPI supplies the model API; your application owns the execution loop. Start with a small planning request, add validated actions, and set a budget for every task.

sections.heading: Choose an API model for your agent
paragraphs: For a first evaluation, gpt-6.1-sol is a lower-cost chat candidate than gpt-6-astra at the checked default-group rates. Claude Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1 provide another pair to test on coding or planning tasks. Compare /gpt-6-1-sol-vs-gpt-6-astra and /fable-5-1-vs-opus-5-5 for prices and evaluation criteria. Those rate differences do not prove which model will complete your task best.

The basic endpoint is POST /v1/chat/completions. Create an API key in the console and keep it on your server. Check tools, tool_choice, streaming and other optional parameters against the chosen model route before depending on them. You can begin with ordinary messages and a planner response while you verify the advanced contract.

sections.heading: Make a bounded planning request
paragraphs: This example asks for a plan only. It does not execute code, call an external tool or create an agent session. Your application must parse the response, validate its structure and decide which actions it can run.
sections.code:
curl https://www.keyoapi.xyz/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEYO_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model":"gpt-6.1-sol","messages":[{"role":"system","content":"Return a JSON object with goal, steps and stop_condition. Plan at most three steps. Do not claim to have executed any action."},{"role":"user","content":"Plan a support assistant that searches an approved help center and drafts an answer with source links."}],"max_tokens":600}'

sections.heading: Implement the execution loop in your application
paragraphs: Store a task ID, user goal, selected model, validated plan and previous tool results. Limit available tools to explicit schemas and authorized data. Treat the model's proposed arguments as input to validate, then run the selected tool in application code and attach its result to the next request using the route's documented message format.

Stop when the acceptance condition is met, a tool fails repeatedly, the maximum turn count is reached or the budget is exhausted. Log each request's usage and each action's result. Avoid replaying actions with side effects when retrying a timed-out model request; use application-level action IDs and idempotency where appropriate. Test a failed tool response as well as a successful path.

sections.heading: Budget for the whole agent task
paragraphs: Agent cost is the sum of every model turn, including retries and repeated context. At the checked Sol default-group rates, a single 10,000-input and 2,000-output turn costs about $0.007354. Ten turns with that identical token mix cost about $0.07354; real conversations often grow, so log actual usage rather than multiplying only the first turn.

Track cost per accepted task, execution errors and human corrections. Summarize old tool output when it no longer needs to remain verbatim, cache reusable application data, and test any cheaper model against the same acceptance rules. Use /model/gpt-6.1-sol for a starting model guide and /pricing for current billing-group rates.

sections.heading: Use a decision model for explicit routing
paragraphs: For bounded routing or triage, /model/cloudflare-clef accepts state plus typed questions and returns choice / noul probabilities through POST /v1/decisions. It does not generate a chat message or execute tools. Your application interprets the probabilities, applies thresholds and decides whether to route, ask for clarification or request human review.
For Claude-class agent budget examples, see /claude-code-api-pricing. The token budget there is an assumption, not a typical session measurement.

faqs.q: Does KeyoAPI run my agent tools?
faqs.a: The chat API generates model responses. Your application manages the agent loop, tool execution, state and acceptance checks.

faqs.q: Do all chat models support tool calling?
faqs.a: Do not assume that. Check the selected model and route, then verify a small tool-call request before deploying the feature.

faqs.q: How do I compare agent models fairly?
faqs.a: Use the same tasks, tools, context and budgets. Compare completed tasks, corrections, time and the total bill including retries, not only per-token rates.

pages.title: AI Story API: Outlines, Scenes & Continuity | KeyoAPI
pages.h1: Build an AI story generator with the chat API
pages.metaDescription: Use KeyoAPI's chat API for AI story outlines, scene drafts and revisions. Keep a story bible, validate continuity and budget input and output tokens per scene.
pages.lead: An AI story generator can use an ordinary chat API for outlining, scene drafting and revision. Give the model a clear brief and a compact story bible, then generate one scene at a time. Keep character facts and plot decisions in your application so each new chapter can stay consistent.

sections.heading: Separate the outline, scene and revision requests
paragraphs: Start with genre, audience, tone, point of view and a target scene length. Ask for an outline before prose so a reader can approve the plot direction. Turn each outline beat into a scene request, then use a separate revision pass to check character names, timeline, established facts and pacing.

Store approved character facts, world rules, unresolved threads and a short chapter summary outside the conversation. Attach only the relevant parts when you draft the next scene. This makes continuity explicit and avoids repeatedly sending every earlier chapter. Keep the original draft and revised version so editors can accept changes selectively.

sections.heading: Example: generate a short story scene
paragraphs: This plain text example uses the listed gpt-6.1-sol chat ID. It requests a short scene with constrained characters and a plot beat. Output length is a prompt target, not a guarantee; max_tokens is a separate token cap. Check for truncation before showing a finished scene.
sections.code:
curl https://www.keyoapi.xyz/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEYO_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model":"gpt-6.1-sol","messages":[{"role":"system","content":"Write an original scene from the supplied brief. Preserve the established facts and avoid adding new main characters."},{"role":"user","content":"Genre: gentle mystery. Audience: adults. Story bible: Mira repairs clocks; her brother Len has been away for a year. Beat: Mira finds a clock running backward with a note signed Len. Write approximately 300 words in third person, ending with a question Mira must investigate."}],"max_tokens":700}'

sections.heading: Choose the model by editorial results
paragraphs: Evaluate a small fixed set of briefs across candidate models. Ask editors to score adherence to the brief, continuity, dialogue, pacing and the amount of rewriting required. The model with the lowest input price is not necessarily the cheapest per approved scene if its drafts need repeated retries.

Use /model/gpt-6.1-sol as a starting integration guide, /gpt-6-1-sol-vs-gpt-6-astra for a GPT-class price comparison, and /claude-api-pricing for Claude-class candidates. Save the prompt and model alongside each draft so an editor can reproduce the workflow. Avoid claiming that a generated story is factually true or that every draft is publication-ready.

sections.heading: Plan the cost of a story workflow
paragraphs: For an illustrative 5,000-input and 1,000-output request, the checked Sol default-group rates produce about $0.003677. Three requests with that identical token mix cost about $0.011031 before retries and any extra charges. Outlining, drafting and revision usually have different token counts, so sum the actual usage from each response.

Expose a scene-length setting and a maximum revision count in your application. Reuse a compact story bible, stop when the editor accepts the draft, and keep failed drafts out of the published story. Audio narration is a separate workflow and charge; see /tts-api if you later add narration.

faqs.q: Is there a dedicated story endpoint?
faqs.a: This guide uses POST /v1/chat/completions with a story prompt. Your application provides the story state, editor interface and revision workflow.

faqs.q: How do I keep characters consistent across chapters?
faqs.a: Store a story bible and approved chapter summaries, attach the relevant facts to each new request, and validate drafts against those facts before approval.

faqs.q: Is AI story generation free?
faqs.a: These chat requests are billed by usage. Welcome gift credits apply only to eligible gift-credit model IDs, are consumed first, and any shortfall is charged to recharge balance. The bare model in this example uses recharge balance; see /pricing for current rates.

pages.title: Study AI API: Grounded Explanations & Practice Quizzes | KeyoAPI
pages.h1: Build a study AI assistant with the chat API
pages.metaDescription: Build a study AI assistant with KeyoAPI: provide course excerpts, generate explanations and practice quizzes, validate answers and track token costs.
pages.lead: A study AI assistant is most useful when it explains the learner's actual material and checks understanding. Use the chat API with a supplied course excerpt, ask for a short explanation or practice question, and verify the answer against the source before showing feedback.

sections.heading: Ground explanations in course material
paragraphs: Select a relevant excerpt from notes or a textbook before calling the model. Give the excerpt an ID and ask the model to cite it in the answer. Tell it to say when the excerpt does not contain enough information. Your application must check cited IDs and answer claims; the prompt alone does not guarantee grounded output.

For longer materials, chunk and retrieve the relevant passages before constructing the request. PDF extraction is a separate step: /model/MinerU2.5-Pro documents an asynchronous parsing route. Do not assume a plain text chat request can directly read an uploaded PDF or browse a source URL. Preserve the original page reference so a student can open the source.

sections.heading: Example: explanation and a practice question
paragraphs: The example sends the course text directly in the message and asks for one short explanation and one quiz item. It uses gpt-6.1-sol on the OpenAI-compatible chat route. Treat the response as a draft that your application validates, especially for graded answers.
sections.code:
curl https://www.keyoapi.xyz/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEYO_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model":"gpt-6.1-sol","messages":[{"role":"system","content":"Use only the supplied excerpt. Cite its ID. If it is insufficient, say so. Give a short explanation and one practice question with a separate answer."},{"role":"user","content":"Excerpt BIO-01: In photosynthesis, plants use light energy to convert carbon dioxide and water into sugars, releasing oxygen. Explain this to a beginner and ask one question about the inputs."}],"max_tokens":500}'

sections.heading: Create a learning loop rather than an answer dump
paragraphs: Keep the question, expected answer and supporting excerpt together. First show the question without its answer, collect the student's attempt, then give feedback and a hint. For factual quizzes, validate the answer key with the source or a teacher-authored reference before using it to grade.

Track the topics a learner has practiced and choose the next item from that history. Ask for a simpler explanation when the learner struggles, but keep the same source facts. Evaluate the system with missing excerpts, ambiguous questions and intentionally incorrect student answers, as well as easy examples. Measure whether feedback identifies the misconception without inventing a new fact.

sections.heading: Budget source context and repeated feedback
paragraphs: A 3,000-input and 600-output request costs about $0.0022062 at the checked Sol default-group rates. A lesson may use several requests for explanation, quiz generation and feedback. Sum actual usage across those steps and verify live rates on /pricing; do not treat one request as the cost of the whole lesson.

Send only the relevant source excerpt and a compact learning summary. Compare candidate models using answer correctness, citation validity, helpful feedback and cost per reviewed lesson. /gpt-6-1-sol-vs-gpt-6-astra covers one price comparison, while /models links to individual API guides.

faqs.q: Can a study AI read my textbook automatically?
faqs.a: This example reads text included in the request. Your application must extract and retrieve relevant textbook passages separately, using an appropriate document API if needed.

faqs.q: Does a source prompt prevent hallucinations?
faqs.a: No. It helps define the task, but your application still needs to check citations and facts against the source, especially before grading or publishing learning material.

faqs.q: Is this a ready-made student app?
faqs.a: This is an API integration guide. You build the student interface, retrieval, progress tracking and grading rules around the chat requests.

pages.title: DeepSeek API Server Unavailable: Causes, Retries and Fallback | KeyoAPI
pages.h1: DeepSeek API server unavailable: diagnose, retry, fall back
pages.metaDescription: DeepSeek API returning server unavailable or overloaded errors? Separate upstream capacity problems from your own code, build bounded retries with backoff, and fall back to a second model on the same key.
pages.lead: A server unavailable error from a DeepSeek endpoint is almost always upstream capacity — rate limits, overloaded nodes or a timed-out request — not a problem with your API key. This page walks through confirming the cause, building a bounded retry policy, and falling back to a second model on the same key.

sections.heading: What server unavailable actually means
paragraphs: DeepSeek lanes surface capacity pressure as HTTP 5xx responses — 500/502/503, timeout-style failures, or 429 when the limit is rate rather than capacity. None of these mean your credentials are wrong: auth failures come back 401 with a clear message. The response usually carries a request id; keep it, it is what support needs if an error persists.
On a relay like KeyoAPI the same status codes mean the same thing: the upstream DeepSeek capacity was unavailable for that attempt. Your client decides whether to retry, and how hard.

sections.heading: Confirm it is the upstream, not your code
paragraphs: Three checks separate capacity errors from client bugs: the same key works on a cheaper model, the error reproduces across several minutes rather than only once, and the failing requests are spread across different prompts rather than one oversized payload. If all three point to capacity, retries and fallback are the right response.
The one-token smoke test against the flash lane is the fastest first check — if this answers while the heavier lane fails, capacity is the issue and a fallback model is the right move.

sections.heading: Build a bounded retry policy
paragraphs: Retry only what is retryable — 408, 429 and 5xx status codes and network timeouts — and cap attempts at three or four. Space them with exponential backoff plus jitter: sleep for min(0.5 × 2^attempt, 8) seconds scaled by a random 0.5–1.5 factor, so concurrent workers do not re-stampede the same upstream. A shared retry budget across your workers keeps retry amplification bounded when an upstream degrades.

sections.heading: Fall back to a second model on the same key
paragraphs: Retries only help when capacity comes back. For hard deadlines, switch model= instead: deepseek-v4.1-flash for cheap classification, deepseek-v4-pro-0813 when you need the heavier lane, or glm-5.3 / kimi-k3 as cross-vendor chat alternatives. The base URL and API key do not change — fallback is a one-field switch in the request body.

Treat fallback as a deliberate route, not a silent rewrite: log which model served each response, because pricing and output shape differ per lane. Live rates for every fallback candidate are on /pricing-list and the deepseek lane is covered in detail on /deepseek-api-pricing.

sections.heading: Run DeepSeek inside agent harnesses without melting capacity
paragraphs: Agent and eval harnesses multiply capacity problems: dozens of workers each firing multi-step chains turn one slow upstream into a self-inflicted outage. Bound the harness the same way you bound retries — a hard concurrency cap on in-flight DeepSeek calls, a per-stage timeout (planner, tool, critic) rather than one global timeout, and a single shared retry budget so a degraded lane throttles the whole harness instead of queueing forever.

Make harness steps idempotent where you can, checkpoint intermediate state between steps, and put the cheapest model on the highest-frequency step. A harness that burns deepseek-v4.1-flash on routing and reserves deepseek-v4-pro for the hard steps survives upstream wobble far better than one that sends every step to the heaviest lane.

sections.heading: Watch cost amplification while you retry
paragraphs: Every retry of a timed-out request risks paying twice if the first attempt eventually completes upstream. For expensive calls, prefer idempotency keys or at-least-once accounting in your own logs, and stop retrying non-idempotent tool-triggering requests automatically — surface those to the orchestrator instead.

Retry storms also inflate spend indirectly: a 4-request retry policy against a 5-second timeout can triple your effective request count exactly when the upstream is slowest. The concurrency cap from the harness section is the guardrail that keeps this bounded.

sections.heading: A practical response checklist
rows: Cut concurrency in half, keep bounded retries
Switch model= to a fallback lane
Honor the limit window, add jitter
Shorten prompt or split the task
Verify with a cheap flash request

faqs.q: Is DeepSeek down right now?
faqs.a: We do not publish a per-vendor status page. The fastest self-check is a one-token request to deepseek-v4.1-flash on the same key — if the flash lane answers, capacity is the issue on the heavier lane, and a fallback model is the right move.

faqs.q: Does KeyoAPI retry unavailable upstreams for me?
faqs.a: No — your client owns retry policy. That is deliberate: automatic retries behind your back make retry amplification and double-billing impossible to reason about. Keep the bounded-retry pattern from this page in your own code.

faqs.q: Which model should I fall back to?
faqs.a: Same-family cheap lane first: deepseek-v4.1-flash for classification and routing. Cross-vendor alternatives on the same key include glm-5.3 and kimi-k3. Compare live rates on /pricing-list before committing a fallback route.
